phonemes.desc: Voiced alveolar lateral [l], unchanged from Proto-Germanic; the name opens as cleanly as English 'low'
Short mid back [o], as in English 'lot'; the Old Norse vowel is short, never the diphthong of English 'low'
Voiced velar fricative [ɣ] — the soft, gargled medial g of Spanish 'lago', not the hard stop of English 'go' — followed by short close front [i]; a light second syllable closed by the vowel

pronunciation.approximation: 'LOH-yi' — two short, even syllables with the weight on the first; keep the o short and round, and let the medial g soften to a voiced friction in the throat, as in modern Icelandic logi.

pronunciation.note: Old Norse Logi is a common noun made person: logi, m., 'flame, blaze', beside log, n., 'flame', and the verb loga, 'to burn with a flame'. The restoration and the ASCII form are the same word — the manuscripts write four plain letters and the ASCII alphabet loses nothing — so Logi is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule. The etymology is transparent in the North; the old scholarly difficulty was never the word's meaning but its neighbor: nineteenth-century philology equated the god Loki with logi, 'flame', on the strength of the similar sound, an equation now abandoned — the vowels differ in kind, the figures never merge in the texts, and Gylfaginning itself stages Logi as the opponent who out-eats Loki at Útgarðr. Attestation and lexicography follow Cleasby & Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary (1874), s.v. logi; Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (1910), s.v. logi; and de Vries, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch (1962), s.v. logi.

domains.title: Fire, Flame, Giant
domains.subtitle: The Trough, the Wildfire, and the Sons of Fornjótr
domains.lead: Logi is the Norse name for flame itself — the common noun logi, 'blaze', walking on two legs into the greatest hall of giants the mythology knows. In Útgarða-Loki's court he is served a trough of meat against the god Loki, and when the two eaters meet in the middle, Logi has consumed the meat, the bones, and the trough besides: wildfire does not chew, it consumes. He is catalogued in the norse pantheon under the domain "Fire, Flame, Giant", and his meaning is the plainest in the lexicon — "Flame".

cards.name: The Trough
cards.desc: The full-length feeding-trough set on the hall floor; Loki clears the meat from the bones — Logi clears everything.

cards.name: The Eating Contest
cards.desc: The one fair contest of Útgarðr: no enchantment was needed — the opponent was fire.

cards.name: Villieldr
cards.desc: 'Wildfire', the unmasking word: what sat down to eat with Loki was flame itself.

cards.name: Hlér and Kári
cards.desc: His brothers in the Fornjótr genealogy: the sea and the wind — an elemental triad with fire between them.

mythology.lead: Logi has one great scene and one great family. The scene is the eating contest in Útgarða-Loki's hall, the showpiece of Þórr's eastern journey in Gylfaginning; the family is the Fornjótr genealogy, which makes him fire brothered to sea and wind. Between them the mythology says everything it has to say about him: he is not a character with a history but an element with a name — and his single appearance is constructed to prove exactly that.

myths.title: The Road to Útgarðr
myths.text: Þórr sets out east for Jǫtunheimr with Loki for company, and at a peasant's farm takes the children Þjálfi and Rǫskva as his servants. On the road they meet the giant who calls himself Skrýmir: they sleep, unknowing, in the thumb of his dropped glove, and Þórr's three hammer-blows in the night — which the giant greets as a leaf, an acorn, and a bird's dropping — will be explained only later. Skrýmir points them to Útgarðr, a stronghold so vast the travellers must tilt their heads back to see the top of it, and vanishes. Every step of the journey is a setup: by the time the company reaches the hall, the story has already taught the reader that nothing here is what it is called.

myths.title: The Eating Contest
myths.text: Útgarða-Loki, the giant-king, declares that no one may stay in his hall who is not master of some art or accomplishment beyond other men. Loki, travel-hungry and never at a loss, speaks first: no one in the hall can eat faster than he can. The king accepts the challenge and calls from the far bench a man named Logi. A trough full of meat is set down on the floor between them; Loki takes one end, Logi the other, and they eat toward each other. They meet in the middle — and there the verdict lies in plain sight. Loki has eaten every shred of meat from the bones; but Logi has eaten the meat, and the bones, and the trough as well. 'And it now seemed to everyone,' Snorri says, 'that Loki had lost the game.'

myths.title: The Unmasking
myths.text: The rest of the evening fails the same way: Þjálfi is outrun by Hugi, Þórr cannot drain the drinking-horn, cannot lift the grey cat, and is forced to one knee by the old foster-mother Elli. In the morning Útgarða-Loki walks the company outside — and when he has told the truth and they turn back, the stronghold is gone. Skrýmir was himself; the glove was the hall; the blows fell on three mountain-valleys. The horn's end stood in the sea, and the tide now answers to Þórr's drinking; the cat was the Midgard Serpent; Elli was old age, whom no one out-wrestles; Hugi was the king's own thought. 'And he who contended with Loki in the eating-contest was wildfire itself' — villieldr — and it was no wonder he made short work of the trough. Fire against hunger was never a contest of the same kind.

myths.title: The Sons of Fornjótr
myths.text: Logi's other attestation is genealogical. Skáldskaparmál, teaching the kennings for wind, names Kári as Fornjótr's son and his brothers as Hlér and Logi; Hversu Noregr byggðist, the legendary preface to the Norwegian settlement preserved in the Flateyjarbók, gives the triad its famous form: Fornjótr had three sons — Hlér, 'whom we call Ægir', Logi, and Kári. Sea, fire, and wind as one old giant's household: the genealogy is not narrative but classification, the North keeping its elements in a family tree, with the sea Logi's brother and the wind his kin.

myths.title: The Flame That Goes Out
myths.text: The word's longest echo is eschatological. When Óðinn asks the giant Vafþrúðnir who will survive the world's burning, the answer keeps Víðarr and Váli in the gods' sanctuaries 'when Surtr's flame dies down' — þá er sloknar surtalogi. The compound welds Logi's common noun to Surtr's name: the fire that ends the world and the flame that eats the trough are one word at two scales. Even eschatology, in Old Norse, is written in the vocabulary of the hearth.

lore.syncretism: Logi's cross-cultural life begins with a mistake and ends with a commonplace. The mistake is famous: nineteenth-century philology, from Grimm onward, heard the fire-word in the god Loki and made Loki a fire-god; the equation is now abandoned — the vowels differ in kind, the figures never merge in the texts, and Snorri stages them face to face across a trough, which is about as far apart as two beings can sit. Its monument survives in art rather than scholarship: Wagner's Loge, the flame-cynic of the Ring cycle, is the conflation set to music. The commonplace is older than any comparison: every tradition that watches fire discovers that it eats. The Vedic hymns give flame a mouth and a priesthood in Agni, the devourer who carries the sacrifice to heaven; the Norse kept the same observation at the scale of a common noun, logi, and personified it once, brilliantly, as the unbeatable guest. Within the corpus his kin are elemental: Surtr of Múspellheimr, whose sword-fire burns the world; Ægir, the sea his own genealogy calls brother; and Loki, the god his name was once wrongly spent to explain.
lore.culturalLegacy: The eating contest is one of the most retold scenes of the Norse revival: the Kearys' The Heroes of Asgard (1857) made Útgarða-Loki's hall a set-piece for English-reading children, and every handbook since keeps Logi's trough beside Hugi's running and Elli's wrestling as the triad of unwinnable contests — fire, thought, and age, the three things no champion beats. The nineteenth century's false etymology had an afterlife of its own: Wagner's Loge, and a long tail of fire-trickster Loki in popular fiction, are children of the conflation scholarship has buried. In Iceland the name never needed reviving: logi remains the everyday word for flame, and Logi persists as a given name. Modern retellings and games cast him as he was written — fire wearing a face, the one opponent in Útgarðr who cheated by being exactly what he was.
lore.extendedMeditation: Names are not merely labels; they are compressed worlds. Logi compresses the oldest observation the North made about fire: it has appetite. The myths give every god a hunger — Óðinn for knowledge, Þórr for food and fight — and then stage one contest where hunger meets its master. Loki is the gods' own appetite, the mouth of the company, and he eats well; no shame attaches to losing as he lost. The lesson the hall teaches is a taxonomy, not a moral: some appetites are animal, and some are elemental, and the two are not the same kind of thing. Unicode restoration has nothing to rescue here — the name arrived whole, four letters the scribes and the ASCII machines spell exactly alike — and that plainness suits him: a word so common the hearth used it nightly, set in capital letters and given a bench in the hall of giants.

lore.archaeology: Logi is a textual figure in the strictest sense: his attestations are the Snorra Edda manuscripts — Codex Regius (GKS 2367 4to), Codex Wormianus, Codex Upsaliensis — together with the þulur, the rhymed name-lists appended to the Prose Edda, which keep the common noun logi among the heiti for fire, and the Fornjótr genealogy of Hversu Noregr byggðist in the Flateyjarbók. No runic inscription names him, no place-name is securely his, and no cult could attach to a figure who is, by definition, an element rather than a person. His material context is the fire itself: the hearth-centered longhouse, the cremation pyres of the Late Iron Age, and the wildfire of the northern forests — the villieldr Snorri names as the truth behind the illusion.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Old Norse form is Logi — the common noun logi, 'flame', borne as a proper name — attested throughout the Gylfaginning manuscripts with a short o and no diacritic; the normalized spelling and the ASCII spelling are identical. In the earlier epigraphic medium, the Younger Futhark, the name would be rendered approximately ᛚᚢᚴᛁ (l-u-k-i) — the sixteen-rune row writes both k and g with ᚴ, so the runes of Logi and Loki are the same — but no runic inscription preserves the figure's name, so the manuscript form remains the primary witness. Because the restoration preserves no distinctive feature the ASCII form loses, Logi is a Tier-2 name: the plain-ASCII logi.com is the philologically complete form — and it is registered to a third party, held outside the PuniCodex collection, and watched for release. The temple is served at /sites/logi/ in the meantime; no owned domain is claimed for this entry.
